label: From Plans to Maps
notes: This chapter, printed pages 205 through 214, attacks the Monge problem by what Villani calls the global approach. We have a Kantorovich plan; we want a genuine transport map. The whole lecture is a single argument: solve the dual, read a c-convex potential off it, and prove its subdifferential is single valued almost everywhere.

label: Monge versus Kantorovich
notes: Recall the two formulations. Monge asks for a map pushing mu to nu and minimizing average cost; Kantorovich relaxes to couplings. Kantorovich always has a minimizer, Monge may not. The global approach shows the optimal coupling secretly concentrates on the graph of a map, so the relaxed solution answers the original question.

label: The Global Strategy
notes: Lay out the three moves the chapter executes. First, solve the dual Kantorovich problem to obtain a c-concave potential psi. Second, restrict to the support of the optimal plan, where psi attains equality. Third, prove the c-subdifferential of psi is single valued for almost every source point, which turns the plan into a graph.

label: c-Convexity and Potentials
notes: Introduce the engine of the proof. A function is c-convex when it is a supremum of cost-translated affine pieces. The optimal dual potential is c-convex, and its c-subdifferential collects, for each x, every y that achieves the defining supremum. Single valuedness of this set is exactly what makes a transport map exist.

label: The c-Subdifferential
notes: Define the central object precisely. The c-subdifferential at x is the set of points y for which the dual constraint is tight. The optimal plan must live inside this set viewed as a relation in the product space. If for almost every x that set is a single point, the relation is the graph of a map T.

label: Quadratic Cost and Brenier
notes: Specialize to the squared distance. Then c-convexity becomes ordinary convexity after a quadratic shift, and the potential psi can be taken convex. Brenier's theorem says the optimal map is the gradient of that convex function. The c-subdifferential becomes the ordinary subdifferential, single valued wherever the convex potential is differentiable.

label: The Map is a Gradient
notes: Make the picture concrete. A convex potential has a gradient field, and that field carries mu onto nu. Convexity forbids the field from folding mass back on itself, so transport is monotone. This is the geometric heart of the chapter: the optimal map is not arbitrary, it is the slope of a convex landscape.

label: Differentiability Almost Everywhere
notes: Explain why single valuedness holds. A convex function is differentiable outside a set of measure zero, by Rademacher's theorem applied to its local Lipschitz property. Points of non-differentiability are where the subdifferential branches into several directions. That branch set is Lebesgue negligible, hence invisible to an absolutely continuous source.

label: The Exceptional Set
notes: Highlight the role of absolute continuity. The exceptional set, where the subdifferential is multivalued, has measure zero. If mu charges no such set, that is, if mu is absolutely continuous, then almost every source point has a unique image. Drop absolute continuity and a map may genuinely fail to exist, which is why the hypothesis is essential.

label: Existence and Uniqueness
notes: State the payoff theorem. For squared distance with mu absolutely continuous, there is a unique optimal map T equal to the gradient of a convex potential, and it is the unique optimal coupling. Existence comes from differentiability almost everywhere; uniqueness comes from strict convexity of the cost forcing the gradient to be determined.

label: From Dual Potential to Map
notes: Trace the full recovery pipeline once more, end to end. Solve the dual, obtain psi c-convex, restrict to the support, differentiate, and read off T equals grad psi almost everywhere. Each arrow is a theorem in the chapter. The global approach is exactly this chain from a number, the dual value, to a function, the map.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Summarize and look ahead. The global approach proves a Monge map exists by showing the optimal plan concentrates on the graph of the gradient of a c-convex potential, single valued almost everywhere when the source has no atoms. Chapter ten will revisit the same conclusion with a local, more hands-on differentiation argument.
